newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW - NKF SAYS EXPORTS GROWING.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NKF SAYS EXPORTS GROWING.

text.p: Telecommunications and energy cable maker NKF Holding NV said on Wednesday its export markets were growing "significantly" because of the company's ability to offer added value to its product range.
NKF in 1995 made a net profit of 40.5 million guilders on turnover of 1.2 billion guilders, with some 24 percent of the turnover generated outside of NKF's "home" markets.
"They (exports) will be significantly higher than 24 percent this year," said chairman and chief executive Tonn van de Laar in an interview, declining to add financial detail.
NKF was selling its basic products abroad but its ability to add value, either through logistical support or by supplying high technology cables was also paying off, he said.
"The fact that our exports are growing is a one-to-one result of being able to change the product mix into products with higher value which are worth selling globally," he said.

"One of the biggest and fastest growers is cables for mobile telephony infrastructure. They are very unusual cables, which look totally different to the classical telecommunications cables," said Van der Laar.
"That product has so much added value, it's so complex to make, has so many sophisticated properties, (and) it's really worthwhile exporting around the world," he said.
Transporting and installing cable in defined projects and taking part in turn-key projects for major operators were other ways of adding value.

"Optical fibre cable as such is always the same, but if you're able not only to bury it but also to install it in overhead powerlines, then you have added value which allows you to get a better margin," said Van de Laar.
Van de Laar said for future stability NKF had to look abroad, where there could be opportunities to cash in on the worldwide liberalisation in power and telecoms industries.
"If you want to be stable and not vulnerable to the decisions of one customer you have to go to more customers which automatically means you have to go international," he said.

"What we see very rapidly is that our customers are becoming international...that's certainly what the future will be, not only supplying in one country but wherever our customers operate and they are operating more and more internationally," he said.

NKF, which has said it saw scope to grow through acquisitions, saw opportunities in the bigger countries in eastern Europe, although the company was treading cautiously, watching political and industrial developments in the region.
Business in the region, where the company has several joint ventures, was responsible for part of NKF's export growth, said Van der Laar.

"For us an important market is in the east bloc where we are building up relationships with specific customers to deliver them the same kind of services we're delivering here in western Europe. A big part of the growth has come from that," he said.

Van de Laar expressed satisfaction with NKF's operating margin in 1995 of 5.83 percent and its 15.42 percent return on equity. "If you look to the major players in our industry, some of our big competitors are in red figures," he said.
But he added there was no reason for complacency. "At this moment it (operating margin) is really good for our industry. It's a task for us in the coming 5-10 years to improve that."

He said continuing liberalisation of power and telecoms industries should provide new opportunities, although more exotic possibilities could exist in the new millennium with the explosion of telecoms technology and anticipated proliferation of traffic management schemes.

"Telecom operators will change from companies who are technology driven, whose traditional activity was to build, maintain and exploit a network, they will become operators and nothing but operators," said Van de Laar.

"That means that the track that we're on (is) to deliver more than just the cable but to go as far as turnkey projects, we see a lot of opportunities to expand continuously there." -- Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
